8  II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
9        The purpose of the CWA is “to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological 
10   integrity of the Nation’s waters.”  33 U.S.C. § 1251(a).  “Section 301(a) of the CWA prohibits the 
11   ‘discharge of any pollutant’ from any ‘point source’ into ‘navigable waters’ unless the discharge 
12   complies with certain other sections of the CWA.”  Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc. v. County of Los 
13   Angeles, 725 F.3d 1194, 1198 (9th Cir. 2013) (citing 33 U.S.C. § 1311(a)).  The National 
14   Pollution Discharge Elimination System (“NPDES”), 33 U.S.C. § 1342, functions as “[a] linchpin 
15   of the CWA’s regulatory scheme,” authorizing “certain discharges of pollutants only if in 
16   compliance with government-issued permits, and impos[ing] related monitoring and reporting 
17   requirements.”  Ecological Rights Found. v. Pac. Lumber Co., 230 F.3d 1141, 1145 (9th Cir. 
18   2000).  An NPDES permit may take the form of a general permit, which “is issued for an entire 
19   class of hypothetical dischargers in a given geographical region and is issued pursuant to 
20   administrative rulemaking procedures.”  Alaska Cmty. Action on Toxics v. Aurora Energy Servs., 
21   LLC, 765 F.3d 1169, 1171 (9th Cir. 2014) (citations omitted).         
22        Industrial storm water discharges in California are subject to the General Permit.  See State 
23   Water Resources Control Board Water Quality Order No. 91-13-DWQ, as amended by Water 
24   Quality Order No. 92-12-DWQ, Water Quality Order No. 97-03-DWQ, Water Quality Order No. 
25   2014-0057-DWQ, and NPDES General Permit No. CAS000001.  The General Permit: first, 
26   requires permittees to implement BMPs to reduce or prevent pollutants in storm water discharges; 
27   second, forbids discharges of storm water that cause or contribute to an exceedance of applicable 
1   develop and implement a SWPPP; and fourth, requires permittees to develop and implement a 
2   Monitoring and Reporting Program in compliance with Section B of the Permit, which includes 
3   filing annual reports with the Regional Water Quality Control Board.  See S.F. Baykeeper v. Levin 
4   Enterprises, Inc., 12 F. Supp. 3d 1208, 1212 (N.D. Cal. 2013).        
5        “[A] permittee violates the CWA when it discharges pollutants in excess of the levels 
6   specified in the permit, or where the permittee otherwise violates the permit’s terms.”  Nat. Res. 
7   Def. Council, Inc. v. Cty. of Los Angeles, 725 F.3d at 1204.  Because “[t]he plain language of [33 
8   U.S.C. § 1365] authorizes citizens to enforce all permit conditions,” any violation of an NPDES 
9   permit can be remedied via citizen suit.  Nw. Envtl. Advocates v. City of Portland, 56 F.3d 979, 
10   986 (9th Cir. 1995).

8        Further, a district court may not combine violations into a single violation for the purpose 
9   of reducing the civil penalties.  The plain text of the CWA provides that any person who violates 
10   the Act “shall be subject to a civil penalty . . . per day for each violation.”  33 U.S.C. § 1319(d).  
11   The Ninth Circuit has interpreted this provision, in light of “the statutory language,” “prior judicial 
12   interpretations of the statute,” and “the general policy goal of discouraging pollution,” as requiring 
13   civil penalties for “each violation.”  See Borden Ranch P’ship v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 
14   261 F.3d 810, 817-18 (9th Cir. 2001), aff’d, 537 U.S. 99 (2002) (emphasis supplied).  In Borden 
15   Ranch, the Ninth Circuit rejected the argument that a district court can consolidate multiple 
16   violations that occurred in a single day into a single daily violation, reasoning that such a rule 
17   would “encourage individuals to stack all their violations into one ‘Pollution Day’ in which 
18   ‘innumerable offenses could occur,’” which would be inconsistent with the language, intent, and 
19   legislative history of the CWA.  Id. at 817.  Defendants’ request to consolidate 9,461 violations 
20   into five violations is more extreme than the one the Ninth Circuit rejected in Borden Ranch.  For 
21   that reason, the Court declines to adopt defendants’ proposal.

13             b.   Economic Benefit from Non-Compliance                   
14        Courts quantify the economic benefit to a defendant from its failure to comply with the 
15   CWA “by comparing the present value of the costs of complying on time with the costs of 
16   complying late.  If the costs of complying late are less than the costs of complying as required by 
17   law, the [defendant] has enjoyed a positive economic benefit.”  See Hawaii’s Thousand Friends v. 
18   City & Cty. of Honolulu, 821 F. Supp. 1368, 1387 (D. Haw. 1993).      
19        Here, notwithstanding the fact that the Court provided the parties with an opportunity to 
20   conduct discovery as to this factor, neither side has offered evidence that can be used to calculate 
21   or even estimate the economic benefit flowing to defendants from their non-compliance.   
22        CAT argues that defendants enjoyed a significant economic benefit from their non-
23   compliance because financial documents produced by defendants show that their gross company 
24   revenue, company profits, and the personal net worth of defendants Scott Farley and Kurt Kernen 
25   have increased each year since 2017, and that over the last two years, defendants have spent 
26   millions of dollars of company profits on acquiring or upgrading vehicles and equipment.  Docket 
27   No. 55-3 at 8-9.  These figures, however, do not speak how much money defendants were able to 
1   save or gain by failing to comply with the CWA and the General Permit since the start of the 
2   relevant time period.

4   $90,000 in mitigation fee fines, $286,000 in expert and attorneys’ fees, and $20,000 in mitigation

6   also do not indicate the amount that defendants were able to save or gain by failing to comply with 
7   the CWA and General Permit since the start of the relevant time period. 
8        Accordingly, the Court finds that it cannot estimate, based on the record now before it, the 
9   economic benefit, if any, that defendants enjoyed from their non-compliance.
